title: Your First Terraform Apply
intro: Terraform manages infrastructure declaratively — same reconciliation idea as Kubernetes, but for cloud resources like servers, networks, and databases.

steps.prompt: Initialize the working directory (downloads providers, sets up backend).
steps.fake_output:
Initializing the backend...
Initializing provider plugins...
- Installing hashicorp/aws v5.31.0...
Terraform has been successfully initialized!
steps.explanation: You run this once per project (and again if you add providers/modules or change the backend config).
steps.why: Nothing else works before this — plan/apply need the provider plugins init downloads to even know how to talk to AWS/GCP/whatever you're targeting. Skipping it gives you an immediate, unambiguous error rather than a confusing one, so it's rarely a real mistake to make twice.

steps.prompt: See what Terraform plans to change before doing anything.
steps.fake_output:
Terraform will perform the following actions:
  # aws_instance.web will be created
  + resource "aws_instance" "web" {
      + ami           = "ami-12345"
      + instance_type = "t3.micro"
    }
Plan: 1 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy.
steps.explanation: This is a dry run — nothing is created yet. Reading this output carefully before every apply is the single most important Terraform habit to build.
steps.why: You could skip straight to 'terraform apply', which also shows this same plan and pauses for confirmation — but running 'plan' as its own separate step lets you review changes calmly, or paste them into a PR for teammates to review, well before you're staring down an actual confirmation prompt.

steps.prompt: Apply the plan to actually create the resource.
steps.fake_output:
aws_instance.web: Creating...
aws_instance.web: Creation complete after 32s
Apply complete! Resources: 1 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.
steps.explanation: Without -auto-approve, Terraform pauses and asks you to type 'yes' — a safety net worth keeping in real workflows.
steps.why: '-auto-approve' skips that confirmation prompt entirely, which is tempting in scripts but genuinely dangerous run by hand — the whole point of the pause is a last chance to notice a plan that would destroy something you didn't mean to touch.

steps.prompt: See what Terraform now thinks exists in its state.
steps.explanation: The state file is Terraform's memory of reality — it's what plan/apply compare against, not the actual cloud API every time.
steps.why: This is different from actually checking the cloud provider's console/API — state list shows what Terraform BELIEVES exists, which can drift from reality if someone changes something outside Terraform. That gap is exactly what causes state-drift incidents.

steps.prompt: Get the public IP output value.
steps.explanation: Outputs are how you surface useful values (IPs, ARNs, URLs) after apply, often consumed by other tooling or modules.
steps.why: Naming the specific output ('instance_ip') gives you just that one value, cleanly usable in a script; plain 'terraform output' with no argument dumps every declared output at once — better when you're just eyeballing everything that got created.

steps.prompt: You're done experimenting — destroy everything you created.
steps.fake_output:
aws_instance.web: Destroying...
Destroy complete! Resources: 1 destroyed.
steps.explanation: Always read the destroy plan carefully in real environments — this is irreversible and, in shared state, affects everyone.
steps.why: There's no gentler alternative here — deleting individual resources by hand outside Terraform would just cause the exact state-vs-reality drift 'state list' warned about above. destroy is the correct, tracked way to tear down everything Terraform created.
